title: AI Prompting Best Practices for Lawyers: Getting Better Outputs
author: Harvey Team

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Harvey accepts the cluster’s core human-led, selective-deployment model and materially develops it with concrete implementation practices: grounding outputs in authoritative and institutional sources, encoding expertise into repeatable workflows, integrating enterprise controls, and retaining lawyer review and judgment.
qs: Flag any uncertainty or areas requiring attorney review.”*  ## Better Prompts, Better Legal Work  Lawyers should use AI to accelerate work, surface issues, and reduce blank-page friction — not to outsource legal judgment.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the application-layer thesis that legal AI creates value through secure, legally grounded, repeatable workflows rather than prompting alone. Its efficiency claims are promotional and unsupported by empirical evidence, so it does not establish defensibility or durable leadership.
qs: The greatest value comes when strong prompting practices are paired with secure systems, trusted legal sources, and repeatable workflows.
Harvey helps legal teams draft, research, analyze documents, and build repeatable AI workflows grounded in legal sources and institutional knowledge.

kp.k: AI augments legal work without replacing professional judgment
kp.d: The Harvey Team's June 18, 2026 article presents AI as assistance for research, drafting, document analysis and issue identification, conditional on prompt quality, source quality and lawyer review. It assigns lawyers continuing responsibility for strategy, source validation and final work product. These are practitioner recommendations rather than measured findings about productivity or substitution.
qs: AI can help lawyers move faster, but the quality of the output depends heavily on the quality of the prompt, the quality of the source material, and the lawyer’s review.
Lawyers remain responsible for evaluating legal strategy, validating sources, applying professional judgment, and reviewing the final work product.
Lawyers should use AI to accelerate work, surface issues, and reduce blank-page friction — not to outsource legal judgment.

kp.k: Structured prompting makes AI work more reviewable
kp.d: The article recommends CLAIM: Context, Legal task, Audience, Instructions and Mode of output. Lawyers should specify the matter, assignment, intended reader, constraints and deliverable rather than use search-engine-style questions. It claims this reduces clarification cycles and improves first drafts; its research, contract-review and litigation-preparation examples illustrate the method rather than test its effectiveness.
qs: Providing clarity upfront reduces the back-and-forth that occurs when an AI system lacks sufficient information to understand the task.
Instead of refining multiple generic outputs, lawyers can begin with a prompt designed to produce a more useful first draft.
The core principle is simple: vague prompts produce generic answers. Structured prompts produce reviewable work product.

kp.k: Source grounding and legal context constrain useful analysis
kp.d: The author recommends grounding prompts in matter documents, authorities, playbooks and internal repositories, while specifying jurisdiction, forum, governing law, procedural stage and legal standard. The proposed mechanism is to supply factual and legal context and narrow the response, rather than rely solely on general model knowledge.
qs: Legal prompts perform best when grounded in source documents.

Contracts, pleadings, transcripts, regulations, playbooks, diligence materials, precedent agreements, and internal knowledge repositories provide the factual and legal context necessary for meaningful analysis.
Prompts should identify the relevant jurisdiction, forum, governing law, transaction type, procedural stage, and legal standard whenever possible.

kp.k: Verification should be built into AI-assisted workflows
kp.d: The article recommends requesting source citations, uncertainty flags, separation of facts from assumptions, missing information and areas requiring attorney review. It also recommends explicit output formats to facilitate human checking and incorporation into legal workflows. These instructions support reviewability, not a claim that AI can independently validate its own work.
qs: Lawyers should treat verification as part of the prompt, not an afterthought.
Distinguish facts from assumptions
Highlight areas requiring attorney review
Structured outputs are often easier to review, verify, and incorporate into legal workflows.

kp.k: Iterative AI supervision resembles assigning work to associates
kp.d: The author uses junior-associate supervision as an analogy for giving AI context, objectives, sources and deliverable expectations, then refining its first output. The article recommends iterative instructions, clarification and review; it does not claim associate displacement or changes to staffing leverage.
qs: When assigning work to a junior associate, lawyers typically provide context about the matter, explain the objective, identify relevant documents, specify the audience, and describe what a successful deliverable looks like.
AI benefits from the same level of direction.
Iterative prompting frequently produces stronger results than attempting to generate a final product in a single request.

kp.k: Suggested applications span litigation, transactions and in-house work
kp.d: The article provides adaptable prompts for deposition summaries, witness inconsistencies, cross-examination, motion strategy, chronologies and authority checking; transactional extraction, agreement comparison, diligence and first-pass disclosure schedules; and in-house playbook review and business-facing explanations. These are proposed task applications, not reported deployments or quantified outcomes.
qs: Review this [purchase agreement] against the [letter of intent]. Identify deviations, retrades, negotiation issues, and provisions requiring business review.
Draft a first-pass disclosure schedule section using the attached [agreement] and [data room documents]. Identify assumptions and information gaps requiring attorney review.
Review this vendor agreement against our playbook. Flag deviations from preferred positions, explain business impact, and suggest alternative language.
Analyze this witness statement and deposition excerpt for inconsistencies, evasive answers, unsupported assertions, and facts that require corroboration.

kp.k: Confidentiality requires data minimization and provider scrutiny
kp.d: The author cautions that even routine prompts may disclose privileged information, identifiers, deal details or strategy. Recommendations include masking identifiers, using placeholders, limiting supplied information, avoiding sensitive inputs in consumer-grade tools, understanding provider data practices and retaining lawyer review. Governance and prompting should be evaluated together before client-facing use.
qs: Even when a task appears routine, prompts may contain privileged information, client identifiers, deal details, personal information, or internal strategy that should not be shared broadly.
Limit prompts to the information necessary to complete the task
Avoid entering privileged strategy, internal legal advice, or highly sensitive business information into consumer-grade AI tools
Understand how the provider stores, retains, and uses data
Strong prompting practices and strong governance should work together.

kp.k: Repeatable workflows can embed institutional legal knowledge
kp.d: The article argues that legal AI use should extend beyond isolated prompts to document collections, internal knowledge, precedent and playbooks, with permissions and auditability. It describes customized Workflow Agents as a way to encode firm-specific standards and review methods, reducing reliance on individual prompting expertise. This is a vendor-authored account of workflow capabilities, not evidence of measured organizational change.
qs: Lawyers frequently need to work across large document sets, internal knowledge repositories, client playbooks, precedent libraries, and matter-specific materials.
They need outputs grounded in authoritative sources and workflows that can be repeated across matters.
Workflow Agents further allow organizations to build customized processes that reflect firm-specific playbooks, standards, and review methodologies.
Instead of relying on individual prompting expertise, organizations can embed institutional knowledge directly into repeatable workflows.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims AI accelerates legal work and improves first drafts and issue identification when lawyers supply structured instructions, relevant sources, and human review.
pts.d: The company blog presents augmentation rather than replacement of lawyers' judgment. Its CLAIM framework—Context, Legal task, Audience, Instructions, and Mode of output—is said to reduce clarification cycles and make outputs more focused, reviewable, and usable. Specifying jurisdiction, source boundaries, output format, and uncertainty helps lawyers verify and revise results. Iteration is said to improve results over a single request. These are present-tense workflow claims, not predictions of lawyer displacement or changes to legal-market pricing.

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims purpose-built legal AI extends assistance from isolated prompts to source-grounded, large-document and repeatable institutional workflows.
pts.d: The author says legal AI platforms support authoritative and internal sources, analysis across document collections, integration with familiar workplace tools, and governance. Harvey is specifically presented as supporting litigation research, early case theories, motion drafting and responsive-document identification, as well as transactional review, diligence, disclosure schedules and negotiation analysis. Workflow Agents are described as embedding firm-specific playbooks and review methods into reusable processes, reducing reliance on individual prompting expertise; the article does not specify their degree of autonomous execution.

pts.k: The Harvey Team identifies confidentiality risks in legal prompting and claims Harvey provides safeguards addressing those concerns.
pts.d: The article warns that prompts can expose privileged, personal, client and business information, particularly through consumer-grade tools. It presents data minimization, masking, provider review and lawyer oversight as safeguards. It separately makes product-specific claims about Harvey's security controls, certifications and non-use of client data for model training; these are attributed vendor representations rather than a claim that prompting is inherently confidential.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers illustrative prompts, an associate-assignment analogy and vendor capability descriptions, not measured evidence of productivity or quality gains.
pts.d: The Harvey Team contrasts vague and structured prompts for Delaware litigation research, vendor-contract review and cross-examination preparation, then supplies templates for other workflows. These illustrate its proposed method but do not include generated outputs, comparative tests, quantified time savings, accuracy measurements, client case studies or cited research. The analogy to directing junior associates provides an explanatory rationale, not evidence of equivalent performance or staffing substitution. Security assertions reference independently audited standards, but the article does not supply audit findings; those references do not substantiate output-quality claims.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern current use as presented on June 18, 2026, with benefits conditional on prompting, source quality, verification and governance; no future adoption horizon is stated.
pts.d: The article describes capabilities available in the present rather than forecasting dates or magnitudes of transformation. Useful results depend on a clear objective, matter-specific material, relevant jurisdiction and legal standard, structured formats, and iterative refinement. Prompt instructions to flag uncertainty and cite sources make checking easier but do not replace human verification. Lawyers retain responsibility for strategy, source validation, professional judgment and final review. Safe client-facing adoption also requires scrutiny of data handling and governance alongside prompting practices.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed benefits primarily concern litigation, transactional and in-house legal teams, with downstream effects on clients and business recipients.
pts.d: Litigators are offered support for research, motions, deposition analysis, chronology construction and cross-examination. Transactional and M&A lawyers are offered agreement comparison, provision extraction, diligence analysis and first-pass disclosure drafting. In-house counsel are offered playbook-based vendor review, plain-language outside-counsel memo summaries and regulatory communications to business teams. Organizations are said to gain reusable workflows reflecting institutional standards. Lawyers remain the accountable reviewers, while clients and other data subjects are affected by confidentiality practices. The article makes no concrete claims about headcount, associate leverage, fees, ALSP competition or access to justice.
